Multi-cylinder dryer section-Corrugated (fluting) medium case study The second section of the TEA analysis was completed to strategically determine the appropriate locations to integrate the RF and US within the dryer section and evaluate the reduction in energy intensity and increase in drying rate, as in Figure 35 of the liner board case study and Figure 36 of the corrugated (fluting) medium. This evaluation was conducted also to evaluate other performance metrics of the dryer section. The experimental RF work, focusing on the reduction in energy intensity and the increase in the drying rate, shows the potential to replace the steam cylinders with RF when using RF combined with convection, compared to conduction combined with convection alone, as illustrated in the first scenario of Figures 37 and 38. However, the experimental US work, focusing on the reduction in energy intensity and the increase in the drying rate, shows the potential to add the US in the dryer pocket when using the US combined with convection, compared to convection alone, as illustrated in scenarios 2 and 3 of Figures 37 and 38. This approach was adopted to enhance energy efficiency and drying performance throughout the dryer section. 46 DE-EE0009395 Figure 37. Proposed locations to integrate the RF and US within the dryer section-Corrugated (fluting) medium The performance evaluation of the linerboard paper machine for integrating the RF and US within the main and after hoods and air dryer of the dryer section were evaluated. Two scenarios for the above case study demonstrated the capability of the techno-economic model and proposed approach to the solution. These two scenarios were carried out by obtaining the actual linerboard paper machine data from the detailed analysis of an industrial report, using four RF and US experimental formulations developed in this project to assess the energy intensity reduction and improvement in drying rate relative to the paper moisture content. The RF was applied with a power of 800 W, while the US was used at average frequencies of 28, 40, 80, and 120 kHz for the first scenario and only 120 kHz for the second scenario. Tables 8 and 9 show the percentage reduction in energy intensity, the increase in drying and production rates, and the increase in reel speed for each steam cylinder group and the entire dryer section. The steam cylinders of the main section in groups 4 and 5 were proposed to be replaced with the RF technology, while the US technology was proposed to be added within the dryer pocket of steam groups 1, 2, 3, and 6.
